source: No official pronunciation statement found; Wikipedia gives no IPA, but FIG-muh is the universal usage by the company, its founders and users.
alternatives: Some origin stories link the name to the Japanese figure brand figma (feeg-mah), but nobody says it that way in English.

source: Figma's 'Introducing FigJam' launch post names the product but gives no pronunciation; it is a Figma + jam compound, usually said with first-syllable stress like other compound nouns.
alternatives: Near-even stress (fig-JAM, like the phrase 'fig jam') is also heard in Figma keynotes.

source: Dictionary.com gives kur-ning, US /ˈkɜr nɪŋ/, UK /ˈkɜːnɪŋ/.

Dictionary.com gives skyoo-uh-MAWR-fiz-uhm, /ˌskju əˈmɔr fɪz əm/: primary stress on MOR, secondary on SKYOO. (Wikipedia gives IPA only for 'skeuomorph', /ˈskjuːəˌmɔːrf, ˈskjuːoʊ-/, with primary stress on the first syllable.)
alternatives: Second syllable may be a full 'oh' (skyoo-oh-) per Wikipedia's variant. Note: bare 'skeuomorph' is SKYOO-uh-morf (stress on first syllable).

source: No dictionary entry with IPA loaded; stress follows the -ic rule and matches Dictionary.com's skeuomorphism (primary stress on MOR).
alternatives: skyoo-oh-MOR-fik.

source: Dictionary.com gives uh-FAWR-duhns, /əˈfɔr dəns/.
Wikipedia's Bézier curve article gives English /ˈbɛz.i.eɪ/ BEH-zee-ay (French [bezje]).
alternatives: Many US speakers say BEZ-ee-ay or bez-YAY.

source: Wikipedia's Bézier curve article gives English /ˈbɛz.i.eɪ/ BEH-zee-ay (French [bezje]).
alternatives: Many US speakers say BEZ-ee-ay or bez-YAY.

source: Dictionary.com gives glif, /ɡlɪf/ (US and UK).
No official or dictionary IPA found (Wikipedia has none); pronunciation sites and common usage give PAN-tone.
Wikipedia says the name comes from 'dribble' (bouncing ideas, leaking work); the extra b was added because the domain was free, so it is said like 'dribble'.
Co-founder Scott Belsky says the name joins 'Be' (be yourself) and 'enhance'; the official stylization 'Bēhance' uses a long-e macron, which points to bee-HANCE.
alternatives: Reduced buh-HANCE / bih-HANCE (HowToPronounce lists /bᵻˈhæns/) is common in fast speech. BEE-hance (first-syllable stress) has no support. Behance tweeted an official 'how do you pronounce Behance' link in 2011, but the link is dead and could not be loaded.

source: A Miro community answer points to Miro's official YouTube videos for 'Mee-ro'; the 2019 rebrand post says the name was picked to be easy to pronounce, and Wikipedia says it was inspired by Joan Miró.
alternatives: Not MY-roh. Spanish/Catalan Miró has final stress (mee-ROH), but the company uses the anglicized MEE-roh.

source: Dictionary.com gives US /gəˈʃtɑlt/ (also -ˈʃtɔlt, -ˈstɑlt) and UK /ɡəˈʃtælt/; Wikipedia gives /ɡəˈʃtælt, -ˈʃtɑːlt/.
alternatives: guh-SHTALT (US too, per Wikipedia); guh-STAHLT without the 'sh'.

source: Wikipedia's Helvetica article gives German [ˈnɔʏə] for 'Neue'; NOY-uh is the English approximation.
alternatives: Sometimes wrongly said 'new' or 'noo'.

source: Avenir is French for 'future' (Wikipedia); Wiktionary gives French /av.niʁ/ with final stress. No foundry (Linotype) pronunciation statement was found.
alternatives: AV-uh-neer (anglicized, first-syllable stress) is very common among US designers.

source: No authoritative pronunciation found (Wikipedia has no IPA); fyoo-TOOR-uh is standard English usage, from Latin/Italian 'futura'.
alternatives: UK fyoo-TYOOR-uh; foo-TOO-rah (German/Italian style).

source: Wikipedia gives Adrian Frutiger's Swiss Standard German name as [ˈfruːtɪɡər] (hard g, stress on first syllable); FROO-tig-er is the English approximation.
The comp.fonts FAQ section 'Pronunciation of Font Names' says Didot is stressed on the last syllable, 'Dee-DOOH' (not nasal); French surname.
alternatives: DEE-doh (anglicized first-syllable stress) is also heard.

source: No explicit pronunciation statement from Rasmus Andersson was found, but Wikipedia says the typeface was originally named 'Interface' (then 'Inter UI'), so it is IN-ter as in 'interface', not the verb in-TUR.
caution: Only the capitalised typeface name; the rare verb 'inter' (in-TUR) is lower-case.

source: Dictionary.com gives gar-uh-mond, US /ˈgær əˌmɒnd/, UK /ˈɡærəmɒnd/.
alternatives: French gah-rah-MOHN (Garamont), with a nasal final vowel.

source: The W3C PNG specification (Section 2, Scope) says 'Portable Network Graphics (PNG, pronounced "ping")'.
alternatives: The letter-by-letter PEE-en-JEE /ˌpiːɛnˈdʒiː/ is far more common in everyday speech (Wikipedia notes both); for TTS clarity P-N-G may be the better choice.

source: Wikipedia gives /ˈdʒeɪpɛɡ/ JAY-peg; Dictionary.com agrees.
Wikipedia gives /ˈdʒeɪpɛɡ/ JAY-peg; Dictionary.com agrees.

Wikipedia: 'The pronunciation as given by the developers is "weppy" (/ˈwɛpi/)', citing Google's original 2010 WebP home page (code.google.com/speed/webp/, now archived). Google's current WebP FAQ does not mention pronunciation.
alternatives: Most developers actually say WEB-pee (web + P).

source: Creator Steve Wilhite showed 'It's pronounced "jif" not "gif"' at the 2013 Webby Awards and told the NYT the soft g is correct (Wikipedia, 'Pronunciation of GIF').
alternatives: Hard-g GIF /ɡɪf/ is probably the majority US usage. Merriam-Webster and Cambridge (US) list the hard g first; the Oxford dictionaries and Dictionary.com list the soft g first; most accept both.

source: Initialism (Scalable Vector Graphics), always spelled out letter by letter; no other pronunciation exists.
Initialism (cyan, magenta, yellow, key/black), spelled out letter by letter; Wikipedia gives no pronunciation.
alternatives: Occasionally read in full as 'cyan, magenta, yellow, black'.

source: Wikipedia gives /ˈwɪziwɪɡ/ WIZ-ee-wig; Dictionary.com agrees (/ˈwɪz iˌwɪg/).
Airbnb's library is named after the animator Charlotte 'Lotte' Reiniger (Wikipedia); 'Lottie' is the ordinary English nickname, LOT-ee.
Wikipedia gives /ˈfæv.ɪˌkɒn/; Dictionary.com (FAV-i-kon) and Wiktionary (/ˈfævɪkɒn/) agree. It is short for 'favorite icon', but the vowel is short 'a'.
alternatives: FAY-vih-kon (from 'favorite') is heard but is not listed by these dictionaries.

source: Initialism for 'user experience', spelled out letter by letter in industry usage; Wikipedia gives no pronunciation.
Wikipedia lists four accepted variants: /ˌk(j)uːbərˈnɛtɪs, -ˈneɪtɪs, -ˈneɪtiːz, -ˈnɛtiːz/; 'NET-eez' is among them and is the most common among practitioners.
alternatives: Wikipedia's first-listed form is koo-ber-NET-iss /ˌkuːbərˈnɛtɪs/; also koo-ber-NAY-teez; 'kyoo-' onset is also heard.

source: Kubernetes 1.9 release notes (official repo) state: 'The canonical pronunciation of kubectl is "cube control".'
alternatives: Widely heard: 'cube cuttle' / 'cube cuddle', 'cube C-T-L'.

source: No official Kubernetes statement found; the docs only explain the numeronym (K + 8 letters + s). 'Kates' is the commonly cited spoken form.
alternatives: 'K-eights' (kay-AYTS) is also common; many people simply say 'Kubernetes' when reading K8s aloud.

source: Wikipedia gives /ˌɛndʒɪnˈɛks/ 'EN-jin-EKS' ('engine x'), matching the project's own description.
Wikipedia gives /ˈɡɪt.hʌb/ with an audio file; hard g as in 'git'.
No formal statement found; follows 'git' (hard g) + 'lab', by analogy with GitHub's documented /ˈɡɪt.hʌb/.
Official PostgreSQL FAQ: 'PostgreSQL is pronounced Post-Gres-Q-L', and links an audio file at http://www.postgresql.org/files/postgresql.mp3.
alternatives: 'Postgres' (POST-gres) is an officially accepted short name; avoid 'post-gree-sequel'.

source: Wikipedia: per the ANSI/ISO standard the official pronunciation is the initialism 'ess cue el'; the language began as SEQUEL (Chamberlin & Boyce, IBM) and was renamed over a Hawker Siddeley trademark.
alternatives: 'SEE-kwul' /ˈsiːkwəl/ is extremely common (and per Wikipedia used by Chamberlin himself); Microsoft people say 'sequel server'.

source: Wikipedia gives /ˌɛsˌkjuːˌɛlˈaɪt/ citing D. Richard Hipp on The Changelog #201: 'I say S-Q-L-ite, like a mineral.'
alternatives: 'SEE-kwul-ite' /ˈsiːkwəˌlaɪt/ is also listed by Wikipedia.

source: MySQL Reference Manual: 'The official way to pronounce "MySQL" is "My Ess Que Ell" (not "my sequel"), but we do not mind if you pronounce it as "my sequel"'.
alternatives: 'my SEE-kwul' is tolerated by the project.

source: Wikipedia gives /ˈrɛdɪs/, citing the Redis FAQ (redis.io/topics/faq) — 'red' + 'iss'.
alternatives: 'REE-dis' is heard but not supported by the project.

source: Grafana staff on the official community forum give 'Grah-fah-nah' (broad 'a' throughout) and point to Raj Dutt and Torkel Ödegaard saying it at the GrafanaCon 2016 kickoff; stress placement inferred.
alternatives: 'GRAF-uh-nuh' and 'gruh-FAN-uh' (flat a) are common in English.

source: YAML 1.2.2 spec opens: 'YAML (rhymes with "camel")'.
Wikipedia notes the 2017 ECMA-404/ISO standard specifies /ˈdʒeɪ.sən/ 'as in Jason and The Argonauts'; Crockford (2011) said 'I strictly don't care.'
alternatives: 'JAY-sahn' /ˈdʒeɪˌsɒn/ is also listed by Wikipedia.

source: RFC 7519 §1: 'The suggested pronunciation of JWT is the same as the English word "jot".'
alternatives: Many developers spell it out: 'jay-double-you-tee'.

source: No official IPA found (Wikipedia gives none); 'O' + 'auth' (from 'authorization') is the universal usage.
Vite docs: 'Vite (French word for "quick", pronounced /viːt/, like "veet")'.
alternatives: Avoid 'vyte' (rhymes with 'kite').

source: No formal statement; '.js' is read as the letters J-S by Vercel presenters and the community.
alternatives: 'Next' alone is common in speech.

source: No formal statement (Wikipedia gives none); '.js' read as letters J-S by convention.
alternatives: 'Node' alone; 'node dot jay-ess' occasionally.

source: Vue.js official guide: 'Vue (pronounced /vjuː/, like view)'.

Co-founder Daniel Thompson on The Changelog #497: 'it's all up to you... a lot of people who have different opinions about how to say it'; name/logo nod to the binary star Alpha Centauri. No canonical form.
alternatives: TOW-ree /ˈtaʊri/, TAH-ree (host: 'like Atari without the a'), TOR-eye (Latin-style, as in 'Centauri').

source: Wikipedia gives /ˈlɪnʊks/ 'LIN-uuks' (Torvalds' newsgroup guidance) and notes his audio recording 'I pronounce Linux as Linux' actually sounds closer to /ˈlinʊks/ 'LEEN-uuks'.
alternatives: LIE-nucks /ˈlaɪnəks/ (older, discouraged); LEEN-ucks (Torvalds' own Swedish/Finnish vowel).

source: Debian FAQ: 'Deb'-ee-en, with a short e in Deb, and emphasis on the first syllable' — from Debra + Ian Murdock.
The sudo project's own intro writes 'Sudo (su "do")', i.e. superuser + 'do'.
alternatives: SOO-doh (like 'pseudo') is very common.

source: Stroustrup's C++ FAQ: '"char" is usually pronounced "tchar", not "kar"', i.e. like 'charcoal'.
alternatives: The C FAQ (c-faq.com/misc/pronounce.html) calls it arbitrary: 'char', 'care', 'car', or 'character'. CAR /kɑr/ and CARE /kɛr/ are both common.

source: Wikipedia 'Daemon (computing)' gives /ˈdiːmən/ or /ˈdeɪmən/; the term came from Project MAC, after Maxwell's demon.
alternatives: DAY-mun /ˈdeɪmən/.

source: Wiktionary lists both /ˈɹɛɡˌɛks/ and /ˈɹɛd͡ʒˌɛks/ (hard-g first) with no preference; no authoritative statement exists.
alternatives: REJ-ex (soft g) is just as common; Wiktionary lists both, hard g first. No creator ruling - kept the stack's hard-g form.

source: Apple presenters read it as 'Mac O S'; Wikipedia gives no IPA but notes Apple said the X in 'Mac OS X' is pronounced 'ten'.
alternatives: Avoid 'mac-oss' and 'macos' as one word.

source: Read as letters I-O-S by Apple and universally; Wikipedia gives no IPA.
Fortune (2024) reports the company's pronunciation 'en-VID-ee-uh'; the name derives from Latin 'invidia' (envy).
alternatives: Common mistake: 'nuh-VID-ee-uh'.

source: Fortune (2024) reports the company's pronunciation 'en-VID-ee-uh'; the name derives from Latin 'invidia' (envy).
alternatives: Common mistake: 'nuh-VID-ee-uh'.

source: No written statement found (Wikipedia gives no IPA); NVIDIA presenters including Jensen Huang say 'KOO-duh'.
No written pronunciation found; the name stands for 'Geometry Force' (Wikipedia, citing NVIDIA PR), and NVIDIA says 'jee-force'.
No written statement (Wikipedia gives none); 'Py' as in Python + 'torch', universal usage.
Wikipedia gives /ˈnʌmpaɪ/ 'NUM-py' (Numerical Python).
alternatives: NUM-pee /ˈnʌmpi/ is common but not used by the core team.

source: Wikipedia: 'Project Jupyter (pronounced "Jupiter")' — from Julia, Python, R, and a nod to Galileo's notebooks on Jupiter's moons.
scikit-learn FAQ: 'sy-kit learn. sci stands for science!'
alternatives: 'SKY-kit' and 'SKIT' are heard but incorrect per the project.

source: Django FAQ: 'Django is pronounced JANG-oh. Rhymes with FANG-oh. The "D" is silent.' (with an audio clip).
Wikipedia gives /ˈkloʊʒər/ 'like closure'; Rich Hickey described the name as a pun on 'closure' with C, L, J for C#, Lisp, Java.
etcd FAQ: 'etcd is pronounced /ˈɛtsiːdiː/, and means distributed etc directory.'
alternatives: 'et-cetera-dee' is jokingly used.

source: Vercel staff in the official repo's discussion: 'It's like "vur-sell"', pointing to Guillermo Rauch saying it at Next.js Conf; the name blends versatile, accelerate, excel.
alternatives: VUR-sell (first-syllable stress) is also heard; stress is fairly even.

source: No official statement found; Wikipedia says it blends 'heroic' + 'haiku' and gives no IPA. 'heh-ROH-koo' is the prevailing usage.
alternatives: HAIR-oh-koo; HEER-oh-koo.

source: Wikipedia gives the French [mistʁal] for the company, named after the southern-French wind; no English-pronunciation statement from the founders was found. Dictionary.com lists both /ˈmɪstrəl/ and /mɪˈstrɑl/ for the English word.
alternatives: MIS-trul /ˈmɪstrəl/ is the other dictionary-sanctioned English form and is common among English speakers; French-style 'mee-STRAHL'.

source: Oxford Learner's Dictionaries (seen in search results; the page returned 403 when fetched) gives MVP as letter-by-letter /ˌem viː ˈpiː/; no word-form reading is in use.
alternatives: Expansion 'minimum viable product' is used in formal speech, but the initialism is the norm.

source: No dictionary pronunciation exists (Wiktionary's PRD entry covers only Pearl River Delta); PM guides such as Miro treat it as an initialism, and with no vowel shape it is spelled out.
No pronunciation guide found in dictionaries (Wiktionary's A/B testing entry has no pronunciation section); the letters are named, with the slash silent.
alternatives: Rarely 'A-slash-B test' or 'A-versus-B test'; make sure the slash is not read aloud.

source: Dictionary.com gives American 'kahn-bahn' /ˈkɑnˈbɑn/ and British /ˈkænbæn/.
alternatives: Wiktionary gives US /ˈkanban/ (enPR kän′-bän′); some US speakers say KAN-ban with the 'cat' vowel.

source: Raymond Chen's Microsoft 'Microspeak' post explains 1:1 (also 1-1) is simply shorthand for 'one-on-one meeting', not a ratio.
alternatives: Must only apply in meeting contexts; in ratios/odds '1:1' is 'one to one'. Lexicon should probably be context-gated (e.g. '1:1 meeting', 'my 1:1', '1:1s').
caution: Means 'one-on-one' in meeting contexts; an aspect ratio ('a 1:1 crop') should read 'one to one' - apply only before meeting-ish words or make it opt-in.

source: Wiktionary gives only letter-by-letter pronunciations: GA /ti ˌɛl di ˈɑɹ/, RP /tiː ˌɛl diː ˈɑː/.
alternatives: Expansion 'too long; didn't read' is possible but changes register; letters are the spoken norm.

source: No dictionary pronunciation found (Wiktionary entry lacks one); spoken usage in OKR literature and talks is letter-by-letter, and 'ocker' is not attested.
alternatives: Plural 'OKRs' = oh-kay-ARZ.

source: Oxford Learner's Dictionaries gives KPI as letter-by-letter /ˌkeɪ piː ˈaɪ/ ('key performance indicator').
Wiktionary gives /sæs/ with homophone 'sass'.
alternatives: Minority readings 'sahs' and S-A-A-S exist but are non-standard.

source: Wiktionary gives General American /pæːs/, i.e. like 'pass' with the 'cat' vowel, parallel to SaaS.
alternatives: British speakers may use /pæs/ (to match SaaS) or /pɑːs/ like their 'pass'; no source found for GB.

source: No pronunciation guide found; in SaaS-metrics usage ('annual recurring revenue') it is spelled out, since 'arr' as a word would sound like a pirate interjection.
alternatives: Sometimes expanded to 'annual recurring revenue'.

source: No pronunciation guide found; it has no vowel, so it is spelled out ('monthly recurring revenue') in SaaS usage.
Wikipedia's lead gives /ˈiːbɪtdɑː, ˈɛb-/ ('EE-bit-dah, EB-it-dah'), with stress on the first syllable.
alternatives: Wiktionary instead lists /iːbɪtˈdɑː/ (ee-bit-DAH, final stress), /əˈbɪtdɑː/ (uh-BIT-dah) and /ˈɛbɪtdɑː/ (EB-it-dah). Usage is split, but all variants keep 'ee/eh-bit-dah'.

source: Dictionary.com gives B2B as 'bee-tuh-bee' (ˈbi təˈbi), i.e. letters with the 2 read as 'to' ('business-to-business').
alternatives: Same pattern for B2C (bee-to-SEE), D2C, etc.

source: Dictionary.com gives B2B as 'bee-tuh-bee' (ˈbi təˈbi), i.e. letters with the 2 read as 'to' ('business-to-business').
alternatives: Same pattern for B2C (bee-to-SEE), D2C, etc.

source: Netflix co-founder Marc Randolph's 'That Will Never Work' glosses CAC as 'pronounced kack', meaning cost of acquiring a customer (Goodreads highlight).
alternatives: Letter-by-letter 'see-ay-SEE' is also heard; the abbreviation CAC is also used for other things (e.g. the French stock index CAC 40, said 'kak karont').

source: Wiktionary gives US /ˈkæɡɚ/ (rhymes with -æɡə(ɹ)), i.e. 'KAG-er', not 'KAY-ger'.
alternatives: 'KAY-ger' and letter-by-letter 'see-ay-gee-AR' are also heard; no authoritative dictionary beyond Wiktionary found.

source: Accounting glossaries describe COGS as said like the word 'cogs' (gear teeth); no dictionary pronunciation found.
alternatives: Rarely spelled out or expanded to 'cost of goods sold'.

source: No English dictionary pronunciation found (Wiktionary and Wikipedia lack one); search summaries and Japanese industry usage ('アープ') support 'AR-poo'.
alternatives: Letter-by-letter 'ay-ar-pee-YOO' is also used. Related ARPPU is usually spelled out or said 'ar-pee-poo'.

source: Wikipedia and Wiktionary both accept 'skew' /skjuː/ and letter-by-letter 'es-kay-YOU' /ˌɛsˌkeɪˈjuː/ as standard.
alternatives: es-kay-YOO is equally accepted; Wiktionary also lists /skuː/. Picked 'skew' because it is the more common retail/e-commerce usage.

source: Compliance vendors describe SOC 2 as said 'sock two' (Service Organization Control 2); no dictionary entry exists.
alternatives: Letter-by-letter 'ess-oh-see two' is sometimes heard. Note: in security, 'SOC' (security operations center) is also said 'sock'.

source: No style guide or pronunciation note found; Wiktionary defines YoY only as a written initialism for 'year-over-year'/'year-on-year', and in spoken finance (earnings calls) the phrase is expanded.
alternatives: 'why-oh-WHY' is used informally by some analysts; British usage prefers 'year on year'.

source: Like YoY, a written-only initialism (Wiktionary lists it alongside YoY/MoM); spoken as the expansion.
alternatives: 'kyoo-oh-KYOO' occasionally; British 'quarter on quarter'.

source: Atlassian's official JIRA FAQ says it is pronounced 'JEEra', based on the Japanese 'Kujira', and the name comes from 'Gojira' with the 'Go' dropped.
An Asana staff member on the official Asana forum gives the company pronunciation as 'ah-SAH-na', which sets it apart from the Sanskrit yoga term.
alternatives: The yoga word is usually AH-suh-nuh (first-syllable stress); a reduced first vowel 'uh-SAH-nuh' is close enough to the official form.

source: Wikipedia gives /ətˈlæsiən/; the name comes from the Titan Atlas.
No official statement or dictionary pronunciation found (Wikipedia gives none); the respelling follows common spoken usage of 'calendar' + '-ly'.
alternatives: Crowd-sourced HowToPronounce lists KAL-end-lee /ˈkæ.lɛndli/ with first-syllable stress. Stress placement is unverified.

source: Zapier's own line 'Zapier makes you happier' (cited from an official Zapier tweet on Zapier Community) says it rhymes with 'happier'.
alternatives: Common mispronunciations are 'ZAY-pee-er' and 'zah-PEER'.

source: Klaviyo's About page says 'It's pronounced Clay-vee-oh', from the Spanish 'clavija' (climbing piton).
alternatives: The company doesn't state stress; VEE stress is inferred from usage. Some third-party guides say 'kluh-VEE-oh', which is wrong according to the company.
